record.paper_title: An Overview of Compact Star Populations and Some of Its Open Problems
record.original_question: What evolutionary relationships connect the observed neutron-star subpopulations, including ordinary radio pulsars, central compact objects, X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs), Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), magnetars, and other hidden neutron stars, and which of these classes are genuinely distinct populations versus temporary evolutionary stages of the same underlying objects?

evidence.quote: most of the Galactic NSs are not pulsars, but instead belong to one of several classes that may be termed “hidden”, which we describe below
These include the central compact objects (CCOs)
the subpopulation termed the Magnificent Seven or X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs)
Another subpopulation which was identified unexpectedly is that of Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs)
A third subgroup of importance is that of the so-called magnetars
Which is the relationship between all these subpopulations?
The idea that some subpopulations are just an evolutionary stage leading to some other type is behind all the attempts of unification

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the observed Galactic population of isolated neutron stars, which is empirically partitioned into several classes distinguished by their emission properties, spin periods, period derivatives, magnetic field strengths, surface temperatures, and ages. These classes include: (i) ordinary radio pulsars (rotation-powered neutron stars emitting coherent radio pulsations); (ii) central compact objects (CCOs), thermally emitting X-ray point sources located near the centers of supernova remnants, with no detected radio emission and inferred weak dipolar magnetic fields; (iii) X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs, the "Magnificent Seven"), nearby isolated neutron stars showing purely thermal soft X-ray spectra, long spin periods (several seconds), and no radio counterparts; (iv) Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), neutron stars detected only through sporadic single radio bursts rather than persistent pulsations; (v) magnetars (anomalous X-ray pulsars and soft gamma repeaters), neutron stars whose X-ray luminosity exceeds their rotational energy loss and which are powered by the decay of ultra-strong magnetic fields (B ≳ 10^14 G); and (vi) additional "hidden" classes of neutron stars that evade standard radio surveys.

Determine the evolutionary relationships connecting these subpopulations. Specifically, identify which of the above classes correspond to genuinely distinct populations of neutron stars with different formation channels or progenitor properties, and which instead represent transient evolutionary phases through which a single underlying type of neutron star passes during its lifetime. Provide a unified evolutionary scheme (for example, a directed graph of transitions among classes parameterized by age, magnetic field strength and its decay, spin period, and temperature) consistent with the observed number densities, kinematic ages, period and period-derivative distributions, magnetic field estimates, and thermal luminosities of each class, and consistent with the Galactic core-collapse supernova rate.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent reviews of neutron-star populations indicate that unification among radio pulsars, magnetars, XDINSs, CCOs and RRATs remains an active open problem. Magnetar-like behavior in some pulsars and high-B pulsars suggests partial unification, and magnetic field decay models link magnetars to XDINSs, but no consensus evolutionary scheme reproduces all observed populations simultaneously.
